newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak CPI seen avoiding quick hit from fuel hike.
newsitem.headline: Slovak CPI seen avoiding quick hit from fuel hike.

text.p: A recently approved increase in regulated motor fuel prices in Slovakia is unlikely to have a direct negative effect on the country's overall inflation, analysts said on Thursday.
But they were quick to add that the secondary impact may reverse the recent favourable trend in the consumer price index (CPI).

The Slovak finance ministry on Wednesday approved a request by the country's sole oil refiner Slovnaft to increase maximum retail prices by about five percent in various petrols and by about eight percent on diesel fuel.

"The increase will not significantly speed up inflation, since motor fuels account for a relatively small part of the current consumer basket used for calculating the consumer price index," Martin Barto, analyst at ING Barings told Reuters.
Slovnaft its proposals for price hikes this year, corresponded to rapid growth in world prices of crude oil.
The company said future price hikes were possible as the upward trend on the world markets is not expected to reverse in the next few months.
The CPI rose 0.9 percent in September, slowing inflation to 5.2 percent, year-on-year, from 5.6 percent in August.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) set its target for 1996 inflation within the range of 6.0-7.2 percent, while the finance ministry in its draft 1997 state budget predicted next year's inflation at under six percent.

Juraj Rencko, a senior economic analyst at the Prognostic Bureau of the Slovak Academy of Science, said the fuel increase would be most felt in all kinds of production depending on energy prices, including the food and transport industries.

"It is hard to precisely say how big will be the negative effect (of the price increase) on inflation, but it is a factor against inflation decline and it will be influenced through secondary factors," Rencko told Reuters.
Barto agreed with the possible secondary effect on transport or food prices, but he said the larger danger for inflation may come directly from food prices.
"Put in a longer-term perspective, it will not be possible to retain the current level of food prices, mainly because of the bad situation in agriculture," Barto said.
Rencko said Slovak agricultue was undercapitalised and neccessary investment was not likely to come from the state budget.

"It will be hard to retain the current food prices, as the sector needs money and it will have to seek other ways how to obtain them than the state budget," Rencko said. -- Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-563-3687
